data.text:
I hate to see this from the CEO of the very respected military forum @WarOnTheRocks Not just because it opens with ad hominem attacks, but because it doubles down on defending an article full of unsubstantiated claims, faulty sourcing, and analytical errors that have already been called out by numerous serious analysts.

I was not involved in the earlier exchanges. But since the author at’d me, I assume he wants my input.

First, on the ad hominem of “Likudnik influencers,” which appears to infer biased analysis based on alleged political affiliation/association/influence with/of a foreign government. This accusation itself reflects a continued failure to do basic fact checking. The irony is that the post responds to Andrew Fox, whose public record includes sustained criticism of decisions made by Israel’s political leadership. Calling him a Likudnik influencer is demonstrably false.

As for me, I do not infer intent from social media posts or selective quotes. I have interviewed Israel’s prime minister, minister of defense, and multiple chiefs of staff directly about war objectives, strategy, and intent. That is fundamentally different from the approach taken in the Milburn article, which relies on inference, misused quotations, and effects-based assertions rather than evidence of orders, policy, or command intent.

This post mirrors the original article in its reliance on bad logic, faulty comparative analysis, and arguments driven by feeling rather than rigor.

“Evidence of civilians targeted.” There is no evidence that Israel targeted civilians. Even the Biden administration explicitly clarified this point. Conflating civilian harm with civilian targeting is analytically sloppy and legally wrong. One can argue about collateral damage thresholds, or whether different forces might have accepted different risk. But asserting intentional targeting without evidence reflects bias, not analysis.

“Senior ministers calling for collective punishment and mass displacement.” If this refers to figures like Smotrich or Ben Gvir, their statements were repeatedly contradicted by Israel’s senior military and political leadership and never translated into operational orders. If it refers to the continued misuse of Gallant’s and Herzog’s statements, those claims have been systematically debunked. This includes direct, detailed rebuttals showing how such quotes are routinely misused to infer intent. Repeating debunked claims does not strengthen an argument. See @Aizenberg55 https://t.co/OFccTv4lQx

“Systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure untethered from military necessity.” No evidence is provided to demonstrate a lack of military necessity. Photos of destruction are not proof of unlawful conduct. As Professor Brian Cox, a law of war scholar, has explained in detail, effects-based criticism is not evidence of illegality or intent. https://t.co/yMhZsn6qqr

“Scale and duration of civilian displacement.” Moving civilians out of combat zones is the single most widely used civilian harm mitigation tactic in the history of urban warfare. One can debate the execution, sequencing, or repetition of displacement. But treating civilian evacuation itself as evidence of wrongdoing ignores both law and history, particularly when Hamas deliberately forced civilians back into combat areas.

“Israeli sources prove the case.” No credible Israeli sources are presented that substantiate claims of intentional civilian targeting or unlawful strategy. Disagreement within Israeli society is not evidence of war crimes.

“Dresden.” I have never used Dresden as justification. I have cited it only to demonstrate how propaganda-driven casualty figures persisted for decades before being corrected. Using historical false equivalence to dismiss analysis is not a rebuttal.

Notably absent from this post is any engagement with Professor Brian Cox’s extensive, point-by-point critique of the analytical and legal errors in the Milburn argument. Ignoring expert rebuttal while claiming good-faith debate is telling. https://t.co/yMhZsn6qqr

The reference to “postwar civilian protection law” appears to conflate the evolution of the law of armed conflict with modern civilian harm mitigation practices. These are not the same. Contemporary mitigation practices emerged primarily over the last twenty years in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Syria under counterinsurgency conditions that are not direct analogies to Gaza, but I have also documented how the IDF has used every civilian harm mitigation procedure created in the last 20 years of counterterrorism and counterinsurgency campaigns and then invented many never used in the history of war - https://t.co/8bZ9pWdvCH

On WWII comparisons, I personally have cited Manila 1945 precisely because it included US hostages, an entrenched enemy, tunnels, dense urban terrain, and massive civilian harm despite the absence of bombing the city proper. Nearly 100,000 civilians died. Context matters. This position also discounts post-WWII history like the Korean War. But the fact is there is no precedence for Gaza - https://t.co/w3qmI0kDKT

Mosul is an even weaker comparison. It was a counterinsurgency campaign, not a cross-border war. It involved no threat to US territory, no US hostages, different ROEs, different time horizons, and vastly different political variables. What is consistently omitted is the cost. Iraqi security forces suffered an estimated five to ten thousand killed to defeat a force of roughly 5,000 ISIS fighters.

Here is a quote from the commanding general of the U.S. support to the liberation of Mosul in 2017, General Stephen Townsend:

“I saw things I have only ever read about in history book… it was the last week…around July 10th… Mosul had been cleared except for a 400 x 400 meter postage stamp…then it shrunk to 200 x 200 … it took about a week to take that…the buildings had been turned into bunkers…rubble 20 to 30 feet on top of the first and basement floors…you couldn’t build a better bomb proof shelter…ISIS was dug in there and he wasn’t giving up…on the last day I watched reconnaissance video feed of the final Iraqi assault…there was an Iraqi bulldozer driver driving through that field of rubble and on each side of the bulldozer was a squad of Iraqi infantry walking along protecting the bulldozer and as ISIS fighters popped up out of the rubble, the bulldozer would turn towards them and bury them whole, infantry walking along would drop grenades in holes and shoot guys trying to fire rockets to knock it out…we found ourselves wondering if we still have flamethrowers in our inventory, turns out we don’t, some armies do, but we didn’t, I couldn’t get my hands on flamethrowers fast or I would have.”

General Stephen Townsend’s description of the final days of Mosul underscores the brutal reality of dense urban combat against an entrenched defender. That reality does not disappear because one prefers a cleaner narrative.

Neither this post nor the Milburn article has demonstrated that Israeli forces used excessive collateral damage given the context, nor that US forces would have performed better under the same conditions. Although, I have publicly stated that the US would likely have fought Gaza differently. But I base that on strategic, operational, and mission variables, not moralized inference.

This post and the defended article continue to disregard all analysis that opposes its narratives. As well of those by numerous senior, experienced commanders, scholars that have visited Israel, Gaza and did their analysis of the above and come to a completely different conclusion. Again, just a few of them:

https://t.co/9nFTeGiAdb

https://t.co/9QTpFUiAeZ

https://t.co/LGFSVb617p

https://t.co/xLQ8uQU4ZC

I agree with one sentence in the post. There are reasonable, good-faith ways to debate this issue. This is not one of them. To include the authors post.

quoted_tweet.text:
The Likudnik influencers on this site have missed the point entirely. They fixate on the photo, noting correctly that other urban battlefields have seen similar levels of destruction. But the photo is not a forensic comparison. It is one piece of evidence among many, set against the repeated claims of "unprecedented restraint" made by this Israeli government and its defenders.

To sustain that claim, they ask us to look away from the images of dead and dying children; from evidence (from Israeli sources!) of civilians targeted; from relaxed ROEs with entirely predictable results; from senior ministers openly calling for collective punishment and mass displacement; from the systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure untethered from immediate military necessity (the presence of so many tunnels wasn't a license to destroy so much); from the scale and duration of civilian displacement; from the obstruction or dismissal of humanitarian access; and from the cumulative effect of thousands of strikes that may be argued as proportionate one by one, but whose aggregate outcome is plainly catastrophic.

You do not get to claim historic restraint while demanding that everyone avert their eyes from historic devastation. No amount of urban warfare whataboutism changes that.

So of course they just fixate on the photo, as if (absurdly) that's the only evidence that can and should be leveraged against the Israeli government and IDF. 

They also reach reflexively for Dresden and other devastations like it, as if invoking one of the most infamous excesses of 20th century warfare were exculpatory. It is not. The world's experience in World War II, including strategic bombing and mass civilian harm, was a major driver of stronger postwar civilian protection law. Citing them as cover for Gaza is an admission that the benchmark being invoked is one the world consciously rejected.

They also reach for Raqqa. but that was explicitly condemned by many as a model of unacceptable destruction. No one is using it as a model for a better way of doing things. When it comes to Mosul, it is certainly not a clean precedent, but US forces did a much better job there than defenders of Israel will today admit (note the Likudniks like to tell you how much of *parts* of Mosul were destroyed rather than the whole city compared to cities in Gaza). Of course large parts of Mosul were destroyed, but much less of it than what we see today in Gaza. Iraqi and US forces also operated under guidance not to use artillery in populated areas and a shift to house to house clearing with light weapons when families were present. And when catastrophic failures happened, like the March 2017 Mosul strike that killed more than 100 civilians, it triggered investigations and operational pauses and adjustments, not celebratory spin like we see today from some of the voices on the other side of this debate.

There is also one big thing missing from the preferred historical comps and cases of those who argue with me here: the enemies were defeated in those other cases. ISIS, the Nazis, whatever past photo of an urban battlefield you want to show me. Hamas has not been defeated. It still is in control of much of Gaza. Israeli tactics did not match strategy. The hostages were returned, yes (not because of Israel, IMHO). But Hamas was not defeated. 

I say this has someone who hates Hamas and supports Israel's right to exist and wants to see a thriving Israel at peace with its neighbors. But, as I noted back in Dec. 2023, while war is always inherently defined by violence, death, and destruction modern professional militaries are capable of more measured, more careful, yet still effective operations against urban enclaves. Many Israelis feel the same way, which is why @andymilburn8 was able to use so much evidence from Israeli sources in his article -- evidence that the Likudniks and their friends in the reject simply because it doesn't fit with their narrative.

There are reasonable. good-faith ways to engage in debate on this issue. Not seeing much of it here.
